findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the exception-handling fallback for review_plan raising LLMError inside both edit --review and claim --review (e.g. catch LLMError, print to stderr, exit 1 matching the existing review-plan CLI pattern) and add a corresponding test stub.
evidence: review_plan docstring (src/rebar/llm/plan_review/__init__.py:424): 'Raises only on a hard context-assembly failure; an unavailable LLM degrades to a DET-only review.'
Existing CLI handler at src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:524-526: 'except llm.LLMError as exc: sys.stderr.write(...); return 1'
Plan text specifies only the verdict-dict mapping path: '_disposition_exit_code(result, indeterminate_code=2)' — no exception path mentioned for either flag
No AC covers the LLMError/exception path for edit --review or claim --review
findings.finding: The plan specifies _disposition_exit_code mapping for verdict dicts returned by review_plan, but is completely silent on what edit --review and claim --review do when review_plan raises an exception (LLMError on hard context-assembly failure, confirmed in the live docstring). The existing review-plan CLI handles this with an explicit 'except llm.LLMError' at src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:524-526. No AC or test covers this path for the new flags.
findings.location: Approach section (both edit --review and claim --review paragraphs); Testing and Acceptance Criteria sections
scenarios: LLM API key is missing or the context-assembly step fails: review_plan raises LLMError; the flag handlers have no specified catch clause; the exception propagates up and may produce a traceback rather than a structured exit code, breaking automation.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to both flag-handler descriptions: 'If review_plan raises LLMError, write the error to stderr and exit 1 (matching the existing _review_plan CLI handler at _llm_commands.py:524-526). Add a unit test stub that raises LLMError and asserts exit 1 and no claim attempted.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that `edit --review` prints the review's finding summary (or at minimum the top-level verdict and reasoning) to stdout/stderr on non-PASS outcomes, matching the behavior already specified for `claim --review`, and add an AC assertion for the printed output.
evidence: edit --review: 'map the returned verdict dict to the process exit status with the disposition mapping' — no mention of printing anything
claim --review: 'the command prints the review's finding summary and exits with the disposition mapping applied to the review result'
AC for edit --review: 'exits with _disposition_exit_code(result, indeterminate_code=2)' — output content unspecified
Help-text AC references non-atomicity notice but not review output content
findings.finding: For `edit --review`, the plan specifies only the exit-code mapping on non-PASS outcomes; it does not specify that the review's finding summary (or any human-readable output) is printed to the user. In contrast, `claim --review` explicitly states 'the command prints the review's finding summary'. This asymmetry means a user whose edit was committed but whose review returned BLOCK would receive a non-zero exit code with no console explanation, while a claim user would receive the summary.
findings.location: Approach section — edit --review subsection; compare with claim --review: 'the command prints the review's finding summary and exits with the disposition mapping'
scenarios: User runs `rebar edit 42 --description 'fix X' --review`; edit commits, review returns BLOCK; shell returns exit 1 but prints nothing — user has no idea why the edit was blocked or what to fix
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the edit --review approach: 'on a non-PASS verdict, print the review's finding summary before exiting' and add a unit-test assertion that the printed output contains the verdict reason for BLOCK and INDETERMINATE stubs.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify which verdict-dict fields claim --review renders on BLOCK/INDETERMINATE/retryable (or explicitly name _render_plan_review_text as the renderer) so the output contract is co-located with the verdict schema.
evidence: Plan text: 'on BLOCK, INDETERMINATE, or a retryable degrade, the claim is NOT attempted — the command prints the review's finding summary and exits with the disposition mapping'
Existing renderer confirmed at src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:583: _render_plan_review_text(result) reads blocking[], advisory[], indeterminate[], coaching[], overlap[], coverage.counts
Plan never names _render_plan_review_text nor specifies which verdict fields to render
findings.finding: The plan says claim --review on BLOCK/INDETERMINATE/retryable-degrade 'prints the review's finding summary' but never defines which verdict-dict fields constitute that summary or names the rendering function to use. The codebase already has _render_plan_review_text (src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:583) that reads blocking[], advisory[], indeterminate[], coaching[], coverage.counts, etc. — but the plan does not reference it. An implementer reading only the plan cannot determine what output to produce for the non-PASS paths.
findings.location: Approach section, claim --review paragraph: 'the command prints the review's finding summary'
scenarios: Implementer writes a minimal one-line 'verdict: BLOCK' print instead of the full blocking[]/advisory[]/coaching[] rendering the existing CLI uses, producing an inconsistent UX and no actionable finding text for the user.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach, replace 'prints the review's finding summary' with 'renders the result via _render_plan_review_text(result) (the same rendering used by the review-plan CLI) then exits with _disposition_exit_code(result, indeterminate_code=2)'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the exception-path behavior for `edit --review` and `claim --review` when review_plan/claim_gate_check raises (e.g., normalize all LLM errors to a retryable-degrade verdict internally, or add a try/except that prints an actionable message and exits 11), and add a corresponding unit-test case for the exception path.
evidence: Plan says 'invoke rebar.llm.review_plan(ticket_id, sign=True) and map the returned verdict dict to the process exit status' — only the verdict-dict path is specified
No mention of try/except, fallback, or user-facing message on exception for edit --review
claim --review similarly does not name an exception path for review_plan/claim_gate_check raises

retryable-degrade (exit 11) implies ADR-0040 transient errors are normalized into verdicts by review_plan itself — but this is assumed, not stated; if review_plan can raise, edit's post-commit failure is silent
findings.finding: For `edit --review`, the plan specifies mapping a returned verdict dict to an exit code but does not specify what happens when review_plan raises an exception (network error, LLM API error, timeout) rather than returning a verdict. Since the EDIT event is already committed at that point, an unhandled exception would leave the user with a committed edit, a non-zero exit, and no actionable message — and the plan provides no fallback, error-surface text, or safe-exit path for this case.
findings.location: Approach section — edit --review subsection; AC: 'edit --review runs the review strictly after the EDIT commit and exits with _disposition_exit_code(result, indeterminate_code=2)'
scenarios: LLM API returns 503 and review_plan raises rather than returning a retryable verdict — user sees a Python traceback, edit is committed, no guidance offered
Network timeout during claim_gate_check after claim precheck passes — claim is not attempted, but the exception surface is unspecified
findings.suggested_fix: State explicitly that review_plan's contract guarantees it never raises (all errors are normalized to verdict dicts with disposition 'retryable'), OR add a bare `except Exception` around the review call in both flags that prints 'review failed: <reason>; edit is committed — re-run review-plan manually' and exits 11, and add an AC unit test asserting this behavior.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify exception handling for `LLMError` and `SnapshotError` (SnapshotError = `_gate_source_error()`) around the `review_plan()` call in `edit_cli`'s `--review` path, mapping them to clean error messages and exit codes consistent with the documented 0/1/2/11 contract (mirroring the existing `_review_plan` handler at `_llm_commands.py:524-529`).
evidence: src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:524-529 shows the existing _review_plan handler catches 'except llm.LLMError' and 'except _gate_source_error()' before mapping exit codes
review_plan() docstring: 'Raises only on a hard context-assembly failure; an unavailable LLM degrades to a DET-only review' — so hard context failures DO raise rather than return a verdict dict
The plan specifies only '_disposition_exit_code(result, indeterminate_code=2)' mapping but does not address the case where review_plan raises instead of returning a result dict
ABSENCE: no mention of try/except around the review_plan() call in edit_cli, nor any specification of what exit code a raised LLMError should produce
findings.finding: The edit --review path calls rebar.llm.review_plan() directly from within edit_cli (_commands/composer.py) but the plan does not specify exception handling for LLMError or SnapshotError in this call path. The existing _review_plan CLI handler (src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:524-529) explicitly catches both llm.LLMError and _gate_source_error() (SnapshotError) before returning a clean exit code. Since edit --review bypasses that handler and calls review_plan() directly, an unavailable LLM, missing credentials, or unresolvable snapshot ref will produce an uncaught exception traceback rather than a clean error message and a well-defined exit code, breaking automation that relies on edit --review's exit codes.
findings.location: Approach section — 'after edit_core commits the EDIT event, invoke rebar.llm.review_plan(ticket_id, sign=True) and map the returned verdict dict to the process exit status'
scenarios: rebar edit TICKET-1 --review --title 'new title' when no LLM credentials are configured: edit commits the EDIT event, then review_plan raises LLMError, propagating as an uncaught traceback from edit_cli
rebar edit TICKET-1 --review when the attested snapshot ref is unresolvable: SnapshotError propagates as a traceback rather than exit 1 with a clean message
An agent script checking `edit --review` exit codes gets exit 1 from Python's uncaught-exception handler rather than the documented 0/1/2/11 codes, breaking the automation contract
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the review_plan() invocation in edit_cli with the same two except clauses the _review_plan CLI handler uses: `except llm.LLMError as exc: print(f'Error: {exc}', file=sys.stderr); return _llm_error_exit_code(exc)` and `except _gate_source_error() as exc: print(f'Error: {exc}', file=sys.stderr); return 1`. Import `_llm_error_exit_code` alongside `_disposition_exit_code` in the lazy in-function import.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the 'gate disabled / exempt' detection in claim --review reads `claim_gate_check(...)['verdict'] in ('disabled', 'exempt')` (or equivalent gate_enabled() call) rather than relying solely on `ok`, to distinguish a disabled gate from a currently-valid attestation.
evidence: Plan: 'when --review is set and the gate applies, call llm.claim_gate_check(ticket_id); if it reports not-ok, run review_plan(sign=True)'
Plan: 'When the gate is disabled or the ticket type is exempt (plan_review_precheck would return None), --review prints a one-line notice ... and the claim proceeds'

claim_gate_check source: returns ok=True with verdict='disabled' when gate off, verdict='exempt' when type exempt, and ok=True with a PASS verdict when the attestation is valid — all three are 'not-ok=False'
ABSENCE: the plan does not specify how to detect 'gate disabled / exempt' vs 'attestation currently valid' — both are ok=True from claim_gate_check
findings.finding: The plan specifies that claim --review prints a skip notice ('plan-review gate not enabled for this ticket; --review skipped') and proceeds when 'the gate is disabled or the ticket type is exempt' — but claim_gate_check returns ok=True in THREE cases: gate disabled, ticket type exempt, AND attestation already valid. The plan does not specify how to distinguish 'gate/type disabled → print skip notice' from 'attestation already valid → silently proceed without printing the notice'. Without this distinction the implementation could either (a) print the skip notice spuriously when the ticket is already reviewed, or (b) miss the skip notice for genuinely disabled gates.
scenarios: Implementer checks `not check.get('ok')` to decide whether to run review_plan; when the attestation is already valid (ok=True) they skip review — but also skip the skip notice, which is correct. However when gate is disabled (ok=True, verdict='disabled') they also skip review — but now must print the skip notice. Without checking the verdict field explicitly, the two cases are indistinguishable.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Approach: 'When --review is set, first check claim_gate_check: if verdict is disabled or exempt, print the skip notice and proceed; if ok=True with a non-disabled/exempt verdict (attestation already valid), proceed silently without review; only if ok=False run review_plan.'

evidence: 5 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the explicit default for the claim_gate_check 'already-ok' branch (e.g., 'when claim_gate_check reports ok, skip the review call and proceed directly into the normal claim path with no extra output') so the executor does not have to infer it.
evidence: 'when --review is set and the gate applies, call llm.claim_gate_check(ticket_id); if it reports not-ok, run review_plan(sign=True)' — the 'if ok' branch is entirely absent
findings.finding: When claim_gate_check reports 'ok' (attestation already fresh), the Approach text says review_plan is only invoked 'if it reports not-ok', but the plan does not explicitly state that the claim proceeds normally when the gate check reports ok. An executor must infer this default rather than read it.
findings.location: Approach section, paragraph (2), claim.py:133 seam description
scenarios: An implementer might add an extra skip-notice, a no-op log line, or a different early-exit when the gate already passes, with no plan guidance.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to Approach paragraph (2): 'When claim_gate_check reports ok (attestation is already current), skip review_plan entirely and proceed directly into the normal plan_review_precheck + claim path with no additional output.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Capture the embedded-prerequisite-verification pattern and the rejected fused-verb alternative in a new ADR (or an AGENTS.md entry) so the rationale is durable and discoverable by future contributors.
evidence: "Alternative rejected: new fused verbs — no OSS precedent, larger surface."
"OSS precedent favors embedding prerequisite verification in the consuming verb (cargo publish verifies by default; terraform apply consumes a staleness-checked plan artifact)"
No ADR file appears in the Scope list; ADR 0040 is referenced for exit codes only, not for the embedded-review pattern.
findings.finding: The plan's architectural decision to embed prerequisite verification inside consuming verbs (rather than new fused commands) — with the rejected alternative explicitly named — is captured only in the plan's ephemeral prose, not in a durable ADR or AGENTS.md entry. Future maintainers will not find a persistent rationale for why --review flags were added to existing verbs rather than new fused commands, making the pattern harder to apply consistently or revisit.
findings.location: Approach section (Context / 'Alternative rejected' paragraph); Scope section (no ADR listed)
scenarios: A future developer wants to add a third verb with a similar prerequisite; without an ADR they must re-derive the pattern rationale or may choose an inconsistent fused-verb approach.
A reviewer auditing the codebase cannot tell why _commands modules reach into _cli helpers for this feature but not others — the 'established pattern' claim has no durable reference.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short ADR (e.g., docs/adr/0041-embedded-review-flags.md) documenting: (1) the decision to add --review to existing verbs rather than new fused commands, (2) the OSS precedents cited (cargo publish, terraform apply), (3) the rejected alternative and why, and (4) when the pattern should be re-used. Reference this ADR from the Scope list.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the flag-triggered review_plan/claim_gate_check invocations emit at least a structured log entry (verdict, ticket_id, duration) on completion or failure, and confirm whether existing review_plan instrumentation is reused or new instrumentation is needed.
evidence: No mention of logging, metrics, or tracing for the new review_plan/claim_gate_check invocations in either flag handler
'invoke rebar.llm.review_plan(ticket_id, sign=True) and map the returned verdict dict' — no instrumentation stated
Testing section covers exit codes and call-order but not log/metric emission
findings.finding: The plan introduces new LLM-call failure points (`review_plan`, `claim_gate_check`) via the new flags but specifies no observability (logging, metrics, or structured event emission) for these calls — no success/failure log, no latency metric, no alert hook. The existing review-plan CLI presumably has its own observability, but the new flag-triggered invocations are caller-initiated and may bypass those instrumentation paths.
findings.location: Approach section — both flag subsections; Testing section
scenarios: review_plan begins returning INDETERMINATE (exit 2) for all --review calls due to a model degradation; operators have no metric or log to detect the pattern
A spike in retryable-degrade exits (11) from claim --review goes unnoticed because no counter is incremented

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm whether `_disposition_exit_code` should remain in `_cli/_llm_commands.py` or be extracted to a shared neutral layer (e.g., `rebar._engine_support` or a small `rebar._commands._exit_codes` helper) now that three `_commands`-layer consumers will import it — the pattern meets Rule-of-Three and the cited precedent (`_help`) is a much lighter import.
evidence: Only 1 existing precedent for _commands→_cli lazy import: src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:562 ('from rebar._cli import _help')
Plan adds 2 more: composer.py (edit --review) and claim.py (claim --review), totalling 3 — Rule-of-Three threshold exactly met
_disposition_exit_code already lives in _cli/_llm_commands.py (line 92), a module that top-imports argparse and multiple LLM helpers — heavier than the _help precedent
The natural shared home would be rebar._engine_support (already used by both _cli and _commands layers) or a small rebar._commands._exit_codes helper
findings.finding: The plan deepens a cross-layer import pattern (_commands modules lazily importing from _cli) that now hits exactly 3 call-sites (transition.py:562 existing + composer.py and claim.py new), meeting the Rule-of-Three threshold for extraction to a shared utility rather than further coupling _commands to _cli. The cited precedent (_help import) is a tiny, side-effect-free utility; _llm_commands is significantly heavier (argparse, multiple LLM helpers). Placing _disposition_exit_code in _cli and having _commands reach up into _cli for exit-code logic reverses the expected dependency direction without a shared neutral home for the function.
findings.location: Approach section: '_disposition_exit_code stays in src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py; the flag handlers use a lazy in-function import'
scenarios: A future _commands module needing disposition exit-code mapping must again reach into _cli, normalizing an inverted dependency direction.
Refactoring _llm_commands.py (e.g. for the module-size policy) becomes constrained by _commands callers that now depend on its internal symbol.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify in the Approach that the `--review` pre-pop must occur between `rest = argv[1:]` (line 512) and `i, n = 0, len(rest)` (line 528), and update the cited range to include the 512-527 block as the actual edit target.
evidence: Plan: 'edit_cli's hand-rolled parser (src/rebar/_commands/composer.py:528-561) treats every --name as requiring a value, so `--review` is handled as an explicit valueless flag checked BEFORE the field loop (popped from argv, bypassing the --key=value pathway)'
Actual code: 'i, n = 0, len(rest)' is at line 528 — the pop must occur in the un-cited lines 512-527 block, between `rest = argv[1:]` and `i, n = 0, len(rest)`.
ABSENCE: the pre-loop block (lines 512-527) is not cited in the Scope or Approach
findings.finding: The plan cites the edit_cli field-loop range (composer.py:528-561) as the insertion point for the --review pop, but the actual insertion must happen BEFORE line 528 ('i, n = 0, len(rest)') — specifically between lines 512 (rest = argv[1:]) and 528. The cited range begins AT the loop start, meaning an implementer reading only the cited lines may insert the pop inside the loop rather than before it.
scenarios: Implementer inserts the `--review` pop check inside the while loop (after line 528), causing it to be consumed mid-parse and potentially swallowing the next token if placed at the wrong point.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the cited range from '528-561' to '512-561' and add: 'the pop is inserted between the `rest = argv[1:]` assignment (line 512) and the loop-init `i, n = 0, len(rest)` (line 528)'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Strengthen the justification for the `_commands → _cli/_llm_commands` lazy import (or replace it): either document why the `_help` analogy holds despite `_disposition_exit_code`'s stderr side-effects, or extract `_disposition_exit_code` to a shared `rebar._commands._exit_codes` (or `rebar.llm._exit_codes`) module that both the `_cli` layer and the `_commands` layer can import without a layer inversion.
evidence: Plan: '_disposition_exit_code stays in src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py; the flag handlers use a lazy in-function import (`from rebar._cli._llm_commands import _disposition_exit_code`) — the established pattern for a _commands module reaching a _cli helper, per the existing lazy `from rebar._cli import _help` inside reopen_cli at src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:562.'

Codebase search confirms zero existing `from rebar._cli._llm_commands import` occurrences in `_commands/` — the cited `_help` pattern is the only precedent, and `_help` is a pure text module (no side effects).
`_disposition_exit_code` at `src/rebar/_cli/_llm_commands.py:92-145` has an explicit stderr side-effect (`sys.stderr.write`) and encodes gate exit-code policy — qualitatively different from `_help`.
findings.finding: The plan justifies the novel `_commands → _cli/_llm_commands` lazy import direction by citing the existing `from rebar._cli import _help` pattern in `transition.py:562`. However, `_help` is a pure text-delivery module with no side effects, while `_disposition_exit_code` has stderr side-effects and encodes CLI exit-code semantics. The two are not architecturally equivalent — the `_help` precedent establishes only that a `_commands` module may lazily import a `_cli` module for text, not that it may import and invoke side-effectful CLI-layer exit-code logic. No other `_commands → _cli/_llm_commands` import currently exists in the codebase. The plan explicitly rejects the alternative of moving `_disposition_exit_code` or creating a shared module, stating 'No file moves', but does not provide a stronger justification for why CLI-layer side-effectful logic should be imported downward.
findings.location: Approach section — '(1) edit --review' paragraph; src/rebar/_commands/composer.py and src/rebar/_commands/claim.py (proposed call sites); src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:562 (cited precedent)
scenarios: A future maintainer adding a new `_commands` module sees the `_commands → _cli/_llm_commands` import as a normalized pattern and begins importing other CLI-layer side-effectful helpers downward, eroding the layer boundary over time.
A test that imports only `_commands/composer.py` or `_commands/claim.py` without the full `_cli` stack triggers the lazy import and pulls in `_cli` dependencies unexpectedly.

findings.finding: The plan asserts '_commands must not import from _cli' as a hard directional rule and specifies an 'import-direction assertion in the new test file', but src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:562 already contains 'from rebar._cli import _help' — a live _commands -> _cli import that pre-dates this plan. A test asserting no _commands -> _cli import in the package would fail on this existing violation, making the AC unachievable as written without either scoping the test to exclude transition.py or fixing the pre-existing violation.
findings.location: Approach section / AC: '_commands must not import from _cli (checked: import-direction assertion in the new test file)' / src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:562
findings.suggested_fix: Narrow the import-direction assertion in `test_review_flags.py` to specifically verify that `_exit_codes.py` and the modified `composer.py`/`claim.py` do not import from `_cli`, rather than asserting a package-wide invariant that transition.py already violates.

findings.finding: src/rebar/_commands/transition.py already contains a live _commands -> _cli import (`from rebar._cli import _help` at line 562, inside reopen_cli). The plan's AC promises 'no _commands -> _cli import' verified by an import-direction assertion in the new test file, but this pre-existing violation is neither cleared nor acknowledged — the assertion test will either silently miss it (if scoped only to _exit_codes.py) or fail on it.
findings.location: AC: '_disposition_exit_code lives in src/rebar/_commands/_exit_codes.py ... with no _commands -> _cli import (checked: import-direction assertion in the new test file)' / src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:562
findings.suggested_fix: Scope the AC assertion to: 'src/rebar/_commands/_exit_codes.py has no import from rebar._cli' (per-file check) rather than a package-wide check, and document the transition.py:562 pre-existing exception.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an Acceptance Criterion for the post-review stale-recheck fail-closed path, e.g. 'claim --review fails closed with the standard precheck message and does not complete the claim when plan_review_precheck reports stale immediately after a PASS review (checked: unit test).'
evidence: Approach: 'on PASS, proceed into the normal plan_review_precheck path and claim (precheck re-checks and fails closed with the standard message if the attestation is somehow still stale)'
Testing: 'it fails closed when the post-review recheck still reports stale'
Acceptance Criteria: no AC addresses the post-review stale-recheck scenario
findings.finding: The Approach and Testing sections both describe the fail-closed behavior when the post-review plan_review_precheck re-check reports stale ('precheck re-checks and fails closed with the standard message'; 'it fails closed when the post-review recheck still reports stale'), but no formal Acceptance Criterion covers this path — meaning the end-state is not verifiable against a named AC and a reader cannot tell which AC this test maps to.
findings.location: Approach section paragraph (2) and Testing section; Acceptance Criteria list (no corresponding AC)
scenarios: A reviewer or CI gate that checks test↔AC traceability will find a dangling test with no owning AC.
If the fail-closed behavior is accidentally dropped, no AC fails — the gap is invisible.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC (and corresponding unit test) that specifies the behavior of `claim --review` when `claim_gate_check` reports ok — e.g., 'proceeds directly to claim without invoking review_plan and exits 0' — so the already-current-review path has explicit coverage.
evidence: Approach: 'when --review is set and the gate applies, call llm.claim_gate_check(ticket_id); if it reports not-ok, run review_plan(sign=True)'

The contrapositive path — gate applies AND claim_gate_check reports ok → proceed directly to claim without running review_plan — is implied by the if-not-ok conditional but appears nowhere in the AC or Testing section.
AC5 covers 'reviews only when claim_gate_check reports not-ok' as a behavioral statement but supplies no checked test for the ok-branch outcome (claim succeeds silently vs. prints a notice).
Testing section: 'claim --review claims on a PASS stub' — this refers to review_plan returning PASS, not to claim_gate_check already passing; the gate-already-ok path is untested.
findings.finding: The Approach describes a control-flow branch — `claim --review` with the gate enabled but `claim_gate_check` reporting ok (review already current) — that has no covering acceptance criterion or test case.
findings.location: Approach (claim --review logic) vs. Acceptance Criteria AC3/AC5 and Testing section
scenarios: A ticket whose review attestation is already fresh and valid; `claim --review` is invoked; claim_gate_check returns ok; the implementer has no AC telling them whether to print a notice, proceed silently, or behave differently from the gate-disabled case.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to AC5: 'when claim_gate_check reports ok (review already current), claim proceeds directly without invoking review_plan and exits 0 (checked: unit test asserting review_plan is not called and claim succeeds).' Add a corresponding stub scenario to the Testing section.

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)
